about: Expected outcomes for the size engine (api/_sizing/engine.js), worked out by hand from each product's published chart and the shopper's profile.

They are reasoned expectations, not real fit outcomes: real validation needs shoppers' feedback. Where a reasonable fitter could pick either of two sizes, both are accepted (leadingAnyOf), and a near tie expects an alternative.
The records are verified, so this suite runs the engine as the endpoint does, without includeUnverified. leadingAnyOf lists the accepted sizes smallest first, not in order of preference.
Chests are in inches unless a case says otherwise. 'ease' means the room the engine aims for (a starting assumption): slim 2-5 in, true to size 5-9 in, relaxed/oversized 10-16 in, around the chest.

cases.rationale: UNIQLO's body chart puts 37 3/4-41 in M. M's garment chest is 23 1/2 in flat, about 47 in around: 7 in of room on a 40 in chest, the middle of true to size.
Relaxed/oversized wants 10-16 in of room: 50-56 in around. L is 50 in, XL 53 in, XXL 55 1/2 in. One or two sizes up from M; XL sits in the middle.
Slim wants 2-5 in of room: 42-45 in around. S is 22 1/4 in flat (44 1/2 around, 4 1/2 in of room); XS is 42 around, at the very edge; M is 47, too roomy.

Revised (strict size labels): a brand and size alone — no product named, nothing measured — is a label, not a garment's measurements. Fynd reads UNIQLO M only as the chest range UNIQLO's body chart gives M (37 3/4 - 41 in), an estimate, and sizes from that body range plus the assumed room for a true-to-size fit; never garment against garment. M leads, S close behind; low confidence. The same shopper naming the product itself is the case below (…-by-link).

The shopper names this very hoodie, by its link, in M: its own published garment measurements of M are the reference (an exact product match), and S and L each miss them by a full size step. The expectation the label-only case had before size labels were made strict.

Revised (strict size labels): UNIQLO L alone is a label, read only as the chest range UNIQLO's body chart gives L (41 - 44 in), an estimate. With no garment known to fit, sleeves that run short are looked for in more length than the chest's pick, which moves the suggestion to XL; low confidence. Naming the product itself is the case below (…-by-link).

L of this very hoodie, named by its link, is the garment known to fit, sleeves included (35 3/4 in). Sleeves running short elsewhere is no reason to leave a known fit; XL would be 1 1/2 in wider through the chest. The expectation the label-only case had before size labels were made strict.

Revised (strict size labels): 'UNIQLO M fits me' in sweatshirts is a usual size, a label — never another product's garment measurements standing in for the shopper's own sweatshirt. It is read only as the chest range UNIQLO's body chart gives M (37 3/4 - 41 in), an estimate, plus the assumed room for a true-to-size fit. M leads, S close behind; low confidence.
Nike's chart puts 37.5-41 in M, and Nike calls the fit standard, which matches true to size. Body chart only, so no better than medium.
44 in is exactly where Nike's L (41-44) ends and XL (44-48.5) begins. Either is defensible; the other must be offered, and confidence is low.
Carhartt's chart gives M for a 40 in chest, and calls the cut Loose: Carhartt's own guide says loose fit runs up to a full size larger. For a true-to-size fit, S or M, with the other offered.
The loose cut already gives the roomy fit wanted, so the chart's own size: M (40). Medium: one chest value per size makes each size's range an estimate.
No record has a women's chart. A men's chart is not read as a women's one.
A fit goal alone says nothing about size.
Fynd has no Zara chart, and a letter size is not a measurement.
A Nike M is a different body in men's and women's sizing; without the line it cannot be read.
A chest measurement doesn't depend on the sizing line: Nike's 37.5-41 still holds 40. The result says the men's-based chart was read.
Nike M is cut for a 37.5-41 in chest (an estimate of this shopper, not a measurement). UNIQLO M at 47 in around gives 6-9.5 in of room: true to size. Low: the chest is inferred.
True to size wants 46 1/2-50 1/2 in around. M (47) and L (50) are both inside, equally far from the middle; chests usually feeling tight tips it to L.
The same chest with no trouble spot: M and L are level, so the other is offered and confidence is low.

Revised (strict size labels): UNIQLO L alone is a label, read only as the chest range UNIQLO's chart gives L (41 - 44 in). The shopper's own 34 in chest measurement is the evidence the engine sizes from, and the two disagree, so confidence is low (the decision policy, api/_sizing/decision.js, answers INSUFFICIENT_DATA "conflicting-references" here). Naming the product itself is the case below (…-by-link).

The shopper names this very hoodie in L, by its link, but measures 34 in, which UNIQLO's chart puts in XS/S. The garment known to fit leads; the disagreement makes confidence low. The expectation the label-only case had before size labels were made strict.
101.6 cm is 40 in exactly: the same answer as the 40 in case, from a measurement in the other unit.
No fit goal in the guide, but the fit profile page says hoodies oversized: read as relaxed/oversized, as in the oversized case.
No fit goal anywhere: true to size is assumed, said, and confidence drops a level.
A waist and hip say nothing about a hoodie's chest, and nothing stands in for one: not enough data.

perSizeAbout: How each size may feel, dimension by dimension (engine output fitBySize), worked out by hand from the published numbers. A class is written as it is expected; "a|b" means class a, could be b (the shopper's chest is a range, and its two ends land in neighbouring classes); null means no class may be given, and the engine must say why.

UNIQLO garment chest around is twice the published flat width (an estimate): XXS 40, XS 42, S 44 1/2, M 47, L 50, XL 53, XXL 55 1/2, 3XL 58 1/2 in. A measured 40 in chest is read as 39 1/2-40 1/2 in. Ease is garment around minus chest; aims: slim 2-5, true to size 5-9, oversized 10-16 in; slightly = up to 2 in outside the aim; no room at all is too tight. Against a garment that fits: chest about right within 1 in around, slightly within 3 in; lengths within 1/2 in, slightly within 1 1/2 in; shoulders within 3/8 in, slightly within 1 in.
These bands are hypotheses. The cases check that the engine does what its documented method says; they are not evidence that the classes match how clothes feel on real shoppers.

perSize.rationale: Several sizes of one product for one shopper. Ease 0, 2, 4 1/2, 7, 10, 13 in against an aim of 5-9: S sits 1/2 in short of the aim at its centre and reaches it at one end of the chest range; L is 1 in past it; XL 4 in. No arm, torso or shoulder measurement exists, so lengths and shoulders get no class.
Same shopper and product, slim (aim 2-5 in). XXS has no room at its centre (too tight), 1/2 in at one end; XS 2 in, at the aim's edge; S 4 1/2; M 7, at the edge of slightly loose; L 10.

Same shopper and product, oversized (aim 10-16 in). M's 7 in is more than 2 in short of the aim: tighter than the fit asked for, not tight on the body. L's 10 in is the aim's edge; XL 13 and XXL 15 1/2 are inside; 3XL's 18 1/2 is just past slightly loose.

A known fitting garment — this very hoodie, named by its link (a brand and size alone is a label, not a garment's measurements): every dimension of every size against L (chest 25 flat, length 28, sleeve 35 3/4, shoulder 20 3/4). M: chest 3 in less around, length 1 1/4, sleeve 1 and shoulder 3/4 in less. XL: chest 3 in more around, length 3/4 more, sleeve 1/2 more (about right), shoulder 3/4 more. XXL: chest 5 1/2 around, length 1, sleeve 3/4, shoulder 1 1/2 more. 3XL: length 1 3/4, sleeve 1 1/4 more.

The chest is not measured, only inferred from Nike's M range (37 1/2-41 in, an estimate), so the ease is a 3 1/2 in wide range. For L it runs from 9 (about right) to 12 1/2 (too loose): two classes apart, so no class may be given.

Body chart only: Nike says M is cut for 37 1/2-41 in chests, which holds 40. That says who each size is for, not how much room it has, so no size gets a class in any dimension; only the chart position is reported.
Carhartt publishes one chest per size (M 40); the range (38-42) is Fynd's estimate and is marked so. No garment measurements: no classes.
